newsitem.title: USA: Mercedes mulls expansion of U.S. assembly plant.
newsitem.headline: Mercedes mulls expansion of U.S. assembly plant.

text.p: German automaker Mercedes-Benz, sensing that its new Alabama-built sport utility vehicle will be a sellout hit, said on Thursday that it may expand production at its first U.S. plant next year.

Mercedes has tooled its new factory here to build 65,000 M-Class sport utility vehicles per year, but demand may be higher. The luxury off-roader's expected U.S. base price of about $35,000 -- not far from a top-end Jeep Grand Cherokee -- has stirred strong interest among consumers. The V-6-powered ML320 goes on sale this fall.

Mercedes' parent company, Daimler-Benz AG, on Wednesday night staged a flashy grand opening show for some 5,000 people at the plant, complete with fireworks, lasers and a Broadway-style song and dance review. But the day after the party, executives admitted that the plant probably will not be able to satisfy demand and they will seriously consider expansion once the production launch is complete.
"If we have a situation that many more customers want this beautiful car, we will find a way to deliver it," Daimler-Benz AG Chairman Juergen Schrempp told a news conference at the plant.
The company's passenger car chief, Juergen Hubbert, said in an interview that Mercedes would probably decide by the end of 1997 whether to boost production.
"If we make this decision at the end of this year, we will have the effect of it in parts next year, at the latest in 1999," Hubbert.
Mercedes has several options to boost output, including adding a third production shift or by expanding the facility, he said. It currently occupies only about 1/3 of a 966 acre-site.

Mercedes' suppliers are already anticipating a production increase. ZF Axle Systems, a German supplier that assembles front and rear axle modules for Mercedes, is prepared to start immediately on a 40,000-square-foot expansion of its new plant in Tuscaloosa, Ala., as soon as it gets the word from the German automaker.
"By 1999, I'm going to have an addition on this building supporting Mercedes-Benz," said George Telenko, the ZF plant manager.

For now, however, Mercedes is concentrating on slowly increasing its production rate to ensure high quality. The plant has only about 850 people building 50 vehicles a day -- less than an hour's worth of production for a typical Big Three U.S. auto plant.
"Quality is not negotiable," Schrempp said. "You have to sacrifice volume for quality."

By early next year, the plant will have up to 1,500 people building 270 vehicles a day, reaching its maximum annual production rate of 65,000. Initially, Mercedes had earmarked half of the production for overseas markets, but Hubbert said Thursday that exports may be cut to 20,000 a year to help satisfy U.S. demand.
Even with expansion plans in the works, Mercedes will take a few years to break even on its $1 billion total investment in the M-Class vehicle and the Alabama factory.

Andreas Renschler, president of Mercedes' U.S. manufacturing subsidiary, said the facility will break even once it produces about half of all the vehicles planned for the M-Class' eight- to nine-year life cycle. Although the total production is undetermined, he estimates that profits may be three to four years away.

Helping Mercedes accomplish its financial goals is a low-cost, union-free environment in Alabama, where many outside suppliers are producing parts at wage rates under $10 an hour. By comparison, General Motors Corp., Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp. parts plants pay workers $19 an hour, plus far superior health care benefits.
The outside suppliers, who produce many modular components such as the axles and fully-assembled instrument panels are providing 80 percent of the value of the vehicle.
The remaining 20 percent comes from inside the Mercedes factory, where wages start at $13.25 an hour and reach $18.10 after two years.

A few miles down Interstate 59/20 from the plant, a billboard from the United Auto Workers union reads: "Welcome to Alabama, Mercedes." Mercedes officials insist that any unionization decisions are solely up to workers.
